impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for method-of-treatment claims permits broad functional genus claims where any member of the claimed antibody genus would be effective for the claimed treatment.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding broad method-of-treatment patent claims for anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headaches, over a dissent arguing the claims were not enabled under Amgen v. Sanofi. The dissent warned the ruling sustains overly broad method claims and undermines medical innovation by allowing patentees to claim vast antibody genera without enabling the full scope.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method-of-treatment claims, particularly in the biologics space, benefit from the court's more permissive enablement standard for method claims, potentially extending exclusivity over therapeutic antibody classes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors and biosimilar developers face broader blocking patents on therapeutic methods, as the ruling may allow patentees to claim entire antibody genera without demonstrating enablement across the full scope of the genus.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the licensed patents such that the licensee could sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether a shift to enforcement-only activities constituted a cessation of business operations terminating the agreement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, entitling TexasLDPC to sue without joining A&M. The court also held that shifting business operations to patent enforcement did not constitute ceasing business operations under the license agreement's termination clause.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from clarity that broadly drafted exclusive licenses can constitute virtual assignments, allowing enforcement without patent owner joinder. The ruling also protects licensees who pivot to enforcement-focused business models.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose the ability to challenge standing based on non-joinder of the patent owner where the license conveys all substantial rights, and cannot argue that a licensee's shift to enforcement terminates the license agreement.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding plaintiff's trade secret damages expert and reducing the jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two damages models it had previously rejected. The court also reversed the district court's reduction of the jury's breach of contract damages award, reinstating the original jury verdict. The court affirmed liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and MUTSA.
impacts.positiveImplications: Trade secret owners benefit from broader acceptance of damages methodologies and the reinstatement of jury verdicts on contract damages, strengthening enforcement against licensees who develop competing products using licensed technology.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal replacements for licensed software face increased exposure to trade secret misappropriation claims and potentially larger damages awards, as courts may be required to consider a wider range of damages theories.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of eligibility for certain patent claims relating to non-uniform constellations while affirming eligibility for others, affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages, and remanded for further proceedings. The decision provides important guidance on the Alice/Mayo framework as applied to communications technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications technology retain protection where claims are tied to specific technical implementations rather than abstract mathematical concepts, and the affirmance on infringement and damages preserves a significant jury verdict against LG.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing industry-standard communications protocols face continued patent infringement risk, and the partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty about the boundary between abstract ideas and patent-eligible technical improvements in signal processing.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a communications apparatus with a coupler matching transmitter impedance to the characteristic impedance of air were invalid for indefiniteness or lack of enablement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds, holding that the claims were not enabled under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a). The decision demonstrates the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds even when the district court's primary rationale is rejected.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the Federal Circuit's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds raised below, providing additional avenues to defeat patent assertions even if the district court's original basis for invalidity is overturned.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face risk that claims may be invalidated on grounds not relied upon by the trial court, requiring robust defense of validity on all potential bases throughout litigation.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent litigation settlement agreement's provision requiring payment 'if any Asserted Claim survives the EPR.'
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a contract interpretation dispute arising from a patent infringement settlement agreement, finding the case turned on state-law contract interpretation rather than a substantial patent law question. The court transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties settling patent disputes should understand that post-settlement contractual disputes may be litigated in regional circuits rather than the Federal Circuit, which may provide more predictable contract interpretation standards.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on patent-related settlement terms face jurisdictional uncertainty, as disputes over settlement language tied to patent proceedings may not qualify for Federal Circuit jurisdiction, potentially resulting in less patent-savvy appellate review.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly dismissed a patent infringement complaint without leave to amend, awarded attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285, and sanctioned plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal without leave to amend, the award of $207,543.60 in attorney fees to Volkswagen as an exceptional case under § 285, and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The court found the proposed amended complaint was futile and that plaintiff had implicitly agreed not to amend its complaint in exchange for an extension of time.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the affirmation of fee-shifting and sanctions against plaintiffs and their counsel who pursue meritless patent infringement claims, reinforcing deterrence against frivolous patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs and their counsel face heightened financial risk when filing infringement suits with inadequate factual bases, as courts may impose both § 285 fees and personal sanctions on counsel.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court adequately explained its denial of Rule 11 sanctions and § 285 attorney fees where the patent holder asserted claims despite PTO § 101 rejections of related applications and a prior court's invalidation of related patent claims under Alice.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of sanctions and fees, finding the order provided insufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent holder that continued asserting claims after the PTO rejected related claims under § 101 and another court invalidated a related patent under Alice.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers gain stronger grounds for fee-shifting when patent holders persist in asserting patents despite § 101 rejections of related claims, as courts must now more thoroughly explain their reasoning when denying sanctions motions in such circumstances.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who assert patents with related claims previously rejected or invalidated under § 101 face increased risk of sanctions and fee awards, particularly where courts are now required to provide detailed reasoning for denying such motions.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly construed the term 'internal diameter' in a patent directed to float tools used in oil and gas well casing operations, and whether infringement and validity determinations were supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's findings of direct and induced infringement and validity of claims related to oil-and-gas wellbore casing tools, based on disputed claim construction of the term 'internal diameter.' The case has significant implications for energy industry patent disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Oil and gas equipment manufacturers benefit from the Federal Circuit's rigorous review of claim construction, which may narrow the scope of competitors' patent claims covering downhole tools.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the energy sector face uncertainty when claim terms have multiple plausible constructions, as vacatur and remand can significantly delay enforcement and increase litigation costs.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming crystalline cabozantinib (L)-malate salt forms, pharmaceutical formulations thereof, and methods of treating cancer satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that the asserted claims of Exelixis's malate salt patents have adequate written description, upholding patents covering cabozantinib malate forms used in the cancer drug Cabometyx®. The decision strengthens protection for pharmaceutical salt and polymorph patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical innovators benefit from affirmation that salt and polymorph patents with detailed specification examples satisfy written description, reinforcing patent protection for commercially important drug formulations like Cabometyx®.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face continued barriers to market entry where branded companies hold valid salt-form and polymorph patents, as the ruling confirms the sufficiency of written description for such claims.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may reach the merits of a § 101 patent eligibility challenge and dismiss for failure to state a claim after already concluding that venue is improper under 28 U.S.C. § 1400(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dual dismissal of an e-commerce patent infringement suit on both improper venue and patent-ineligibility grounds. The court held that the district court did not err by addressing and ruling on § 101 eligibility even after determining venue was improper, allowing the eligibility determination to stand.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from courts' ability to reach § 101 eligibility even after finding improper venue, potentially creating preclusive invalidity determinations that prevent re-filing in other districts.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities face the risk that courts will issue merits-based invalidity rulings alongside venue dismissals, potentially precluding re-assertion of the same patents in properly venued forums.
